title: Ungulate use before and after utility‐scale solar development
content:
We found multiple lines of evidence that indicate pronghorn use declined near an 80-MW solar facility. Our study suggests that indirect habitat loss could exacerbate the impacts of solar development on ungulates and potentially complicate the effectiveness of design-based mitigation measures that assume animals will readily utilize habitats adjacent to solar projects.


Abstract

The global transition to renewable energy has large land requirements that can impact local wildlife populations. A clear understanding of whether, or to what degree, wildlife avoid utility-scale solar energy (USSE) development is critical for effective mitigation and planning. This is particularly important for ungulates and other large mammals that cannot move through USSE perimeter fences and instead, rely on design-based mitigation measures (e.g. movement corridors) to minimize impacts and retain connectivity. Using a suite of complementary metrics and fine-scale global positioning system (GPS) data collected 6 months before and 5 years after development, we found multiple lines of evidence that non-migratory pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) avoid USSE. Absent avoidance behaviours, we expected pronghorn use to be similar during pre- and post-construction periods. Yet, we found weekly encounter rates along the USSE perimeter were more than 3× lower after construction. The pattern of less pronghorn use near the USSE extended >1 km. For example, 10% of all pre-construction GPS locations occurred within 0.75 km of the USSE, but the distance needed to contain a similar proportion of locations after construction ranged from 1.65 to 1.75 km. Relatedly, the amount of high-use pronghorn habitat surrounding the USSE declined after development, with the steepest declines (40%–60%) occurring within 1 km of the solar site. When key environmental covariates were accounted for in a resource selection framework, pronghorn preferred to use habitats near the location of the USSE prior to construction, but following construction probability of use was highest at 1.50 km away from the USSE. Practical implication. The direct loss of habitat and reduced connectivity associated with USSE pose serious challenges for ungulate populations. Our results suggest avoidance behaviours could exacerbate the impacts to ungulates through indirect habitat loss and potentially complicate the effectiveness of design-based mitigation measures that assume animals will readily utilize habitats adjacent to USSE.
